overview: A two-page U.S. Department of State “List of Papers,” compiled on October 1, 1945, indexing records filed under Japanese periodicals. Its entries summarize and cross-reference diplomatic reporting from roughly 1940–1942 concerning the suppression of Gaiko Jiho over an article on the China Incident, material published in Japanese Abroad, Japan News Week, Nippon, and the OCR-rendered Japan Wine View, requests for Nagao Ariga’s study of the Russo-Japanese War, the acquisition of Japanese publications through Soviet channels, and the wartime curtailment of leading Japanese magazines. One anomalous entry concerns the Japanese hospital ship Op ten Noort and broader hospital-ship policy.

subfiles.title: Department of State List of Papers: Periodicals—Japan
subfiles.about: An administrative inventory summarizes and cross-references diplomatic records concerning Japanese periodicals, publications, and related wartime press matters.
subfiles.summary: The first page lists reports on the Home Office’s suppression of Gaiko Jiho, foreign diplomatic letters printed in Japanese Abroad, a Japan News Week editorial connected with a Foreign Minister’s address, and an issue of the illustrated quarterly Nippon. The continuation records complaints about the non-delivery of Japan Wine View in the United States, a request for additional copies of Nagao Ariga’s La Guerre Russo-Japonaise, and the ordering of Japanese publications through a Soviet agency. It also notes the Navy Department’s position on the hospital ship Op ten Noort and a Moscow telegram reporting the curtailment of leading magazines in Japan. Several entries direct the reader to records filed under other decimal classifications.

interest: The inventory is useful as a compact map of State Department reporting on Japan’s wartime print culture, censorship, propaganda, and the international circulation of Japanese publications. It connects press controls inside Japan with diplomatic reactions abroad, including material involving American, British, Hungarian, and Soviet representatives. Its cross-references also reveal how related evidence was dispersed across the Department’s decimal filing system, while the unexpected Op ten Noort entry illustrates the occasional looseness or accidental admixture of subjects in archival files.
